title: Huawei Becomes Proxy for Public Criticism of Party-State
zh_title: 华为成为公开批评党国的代理人
summary: 内容摘要：北京已使华为成为中华人民共和国（PRC）高科技行业的旗手，质疑该公司的内容经常遭到投诉和删除。因此，嘲笑华为已成为公众批评党国的代表。 10月8日发布的第三方测试显示，华为推出的汽车Maextro V800的制动踏板支架在反复紧急制动下发生断裂。随后测试视频从多个平台消失，网上的嘲讽从刹车转向审查，转向华为的政治
content:
内容摘要：北京已使华为成为中华人民共和国（PRC）高科技行业的旗手，质疑该公司的内容经常遭到投诉和删除。因此，嘲笑华为已成为公众批评党国的代表。 10月8日发布的第三方测试显示，华为推出的汽车Maextro V800的制动踏板支架在反复紧急制动下发生断裂。随后，测试视频从多个平台上消失，网上的嘲讽也从刹车转向了审查，转向了华为的政治支持者。保护华为的努力进一步传播了嘲笑。一些官方账号公开敦促该公司接受讨论，表明部分系统认为批评华为是可以的。自刹车踏板事件以来，中央官方媒体拒绝为华为辩护，中央领导层可能会在未来的宣传中与该公司保持距离。 10月8日，中国汽车评论平台“懂车帝”发布了一段制动测试视频，视频中三辆新款尊界V800从时速100公里处反复急停。三者的制动踏板支架均断裂（中央人民广播电台，10 月 8 日）。 [1] 该车由安徽江淮汽车（JAC；江淮汽车）制造，由华为于 8 月推出，价格从人民币 766,000 元（114,000 美元）到 102 万元人民币（150,000 美元）不等。
其官网将其安全设计宣传为“多重冗余，稳定如泰山”，并指出车辆架构包括制动、转向、计算、感知、定位、交互、通信、供电等冗余（HIMA，10月9日访问）。当日交易中，江淮汽车股价跌至熔断跌停，次日开盘后再次跌至熔断跌停（《21世纪经济报道》，10月9日）。这个故事很快就变成了审查制度的故事。当晚起，测试视频在中国领先的视频分享平台哔哩哔哩上显示“稿件失效”，微信频道则显示公告称，经用户投诉和平台审核，发现该视频含有违反平台规则的内容。该通知未说明投诉人及原因（新黄河网10月9日）。次日，网友发现抖音、哔哩哔哩、微博等平台的原视频和多条转发已被删除。在X账号“李老师不是你老师”转发的中国境内用户评论中，有一条写道：“不得不说，华为代表党实现了对理论喉舌和舆论战线的坚强领导”（X/@whyyoutouzhele，10月9日）。
[2] 该评论借用了党控制媒体的词汇，并将其应用于在中国拥有特殊地位的华为公司。官员们将华为视为受美国打压的中国高科技公司的代表，其批评者经常被指控抹黑国内品牌，质疑其的网络内容经常被审查机构删除。这种代表当局的特殊保护态度，加上直接向政权提出审查制度、特权和不平等正义问题所带来的困难，导致华为成为代理人。

【原文 English Original】
Executive Summary: Beijing has made Huawei the standard-bearer of the high-tech sector in the People’s Republic of China (PRC), and content that questions the company is routinely met with complaints and takedowns. Mocking Huawei has therefore become a proxy for public criticism of the Party-state. A third-party test published on October 8 showed the brake pedal bracket of the Maextro V800, a car launched by Huawei, breaking under repeated emergency braking. The test video then disappeared from multiple platforms, and online mockery moved from the brakes to censorship and to Huawei’s political backers. Efforts to shield Huawei have spread the mockery further. Some official accounts have publicly urged the company to accept discussion, indicating that parts of the system regard criticism of Huawei as permissible. Since the brake pedal incident, central state media have declined to come to Huawei’s defense, and the central leadership may keep its distance from the company in future propaganda. On October 8, Dongchedi (懂车帝), a car review platform in the People’s Republic of China (PRC), published a video of a brake test, where three new Maextro (尊界) V800s made repeated emergency stops from 100 kilometers per hour. The brake pedal bracket broke on all three ( China National Radio , October 8).  [1] The car, built by Anhui Jianghuai Automobile (JAC; 江淮汽车), was launched by Huawei in August at prices from renminbi (RMB) 766,000 ($114,000) to RMB 1.02 million ($150,000). Its official website advertises the safety design as “multiple redundancies, as stable as Mount Tai” (多重冗余，稳若泰山) and states that the vehicle’s architecture includes redundancy in braking, steering, computing, perception, positioning, interaction, communications, and power supply ( HIMA , accessed October 9). JAC’s shares fell to the circuit-breaker limit during trading that day and again once markets opened the following day ( 21st Century Business Herald , October 9). The story quickly turned into one of censorship. From late that night, the test video displayed the message “submission invalid” (稿件失效) on Bilibili, a leading PRC video-sharing platform, while WeChat Channels showed a notice stating that, following user complaints and platform review, the video had been found to contain content that violated the platform rules. The notice left both the complainant and the reason unstated ( Xinhuanghe , October 9). By the next day, Internet users found that the original video and many reposts had been removed from Douyin, Bilibili, Weibo, and other platforms. Among comments from users inside the PRC relayed by the X account “Teacher Li Is Not Your Teacher” (李老师不是你老师), one read, “it must be said that Huawei has achieved, on the Party’s behalf, strong leadership over the theoretical mouthpieces and the public opinion front” (不得不说，华为替党做到了对理论喉舌舆论阵地的坚强领导) ( X/@whyyoutouzhele , October 9).  [2] The comment borrows the vocabulary of Party control over the media and applies it to a company, Huawei, that holds special status in the PRC. Officials treat Huawei as the representative of Chinese high-tech firms suppressed by the United States, its critics are often accused of smearing domestic brands, and online content that questions it is frequently taken down by censors. This particular protectiveness on behalf of the authorities, coupled with the difficulties entailed in raising issues of censorship, privilege, and unequal justice directly with the regime, has led to Huawei becoming a proxy for public criticism of the Party-state. Beijing Makes Huawei a National Symbol U.S. sanctions turned Huawei into an object of patriotic consumption. In May 2019, the U.S. Department of Commerce added Huawei to the Entity List, restricting sales by U.S. firms to the company ( Federal Register , May 21, 2019). Promotions and patriotic sentiment then drove a surge in its smartphone sales at home ( Reuters , August 5, 2019). Huawei founder Ren Zhengfei (任正非) remarked wryly at the time that “one cannot say that using Huawei products is patriotic and that not using them is unpatriotic” (不能说用华为产品就爱国，不用就不爱国) ( BBC , May 21, 2019). During the Meng Wanzhou (孟晚舟) affair, officials presented Huawei’s plight as the nation’s plight. On September 25, 2021, Meng, who is Huawei’s chief financial officer and Ren’s daughter, returned to Shenzhen after nearly three years of detention in Canada. Xinhua headlined its report with her words at the airport, “If faith has a color, it must be China red!” (如果信念有颜色，那一定是中国红！) ( Xinhua , September 25, 2021). Two days later, a Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) spokesperson stated that the case’s “purpose was to suppress Chinese high-tech enterprises represented by Huawei” (目的是打压以华为为代表的中国高技术企业) ( MFA , September 27, 2021). Canadian and U.S. authorities had initially arrested her for charges of wire fraud that violated U.S. sanctions on Iran, though these were dismissed once a plea deal had been reached. The state also backs Huawei with money and political favor. Materials from the U.S. Semiconductor Industry Association reported by Bloomberg indicate that Huawei obtained about $30 billion from the central government and the Shenzhen municipal government ( Bloomberg , August 23, 2023). In February 2025, at a symposium on private enterprise chaired by General Secretary Xi Jinping, Ren was listed first among the six business leaders who spoke ( Xinhua , February 19, 2025). In recent years, private technology firms in the PRC have generally aligned themselves with national strategy before receiving explicit instructions ( China Brief , March 20). Huawei has gone further, however, and has become part of the national narrative itself. This status also shields Huawei from criticism. One PRC technology commentator has said outright that Huawei long enjoyed a degree of protection in public opinion under the national narrative ( HK01 , August 6). In late 2025, the well-known internet personality Luo Yonghao (罗永浩) was likewise accused of “smearing national industry” (黑民族产业) after he joked about “far ahead” (遥遥领先), a catchphrase from Huawei’s product launches ( Sina Finance , January 3). After the brake incident, an industry insider still publicly questioned “certain media outlets that gain traffic at the expense of Chinese brands’ reputations” (个别媒体以牺牲中国品牌的口碑获取流量) ( JRJ , October 9). In an atmosphere that binds Huawei tightly to patriotism, questioning its products is easily cast as opposing the country. Pushback Ranges From Parody to Political Satire Criticizing a company is far safer in the PRC than criticizing the Party or the government. Consumer complaints about product quality are an officially recognized right, and China Central Television (CCTV) devotes a broadcast every March 15 to exposing errant firms. Huawei is at once a company open to consumer complaint and one that officials treat as a representative of the nation. Those who mock it can therefore claim that they are simply discussing product quality. Public pushback against Huawei falls into roughly three categories. The first is parody, which targets the company’s marketing language. For instance, in July, Internet users decided that the “wah-wah” sound a traditional toy, the bamboo cicada (竹知了), makes when shaken resembled both the voice of Huawei executive Yu Chengdong (余承东) at product launches and the gasps of his audiences. Borrowing his description of the Aito (问界) M9 as “the best SUV under RMB 10 million” (1000万以内最好的SUV), they dubbed the toy “the best toy under RMB 10 million” (一千万以内最好的玩具) ( 21st Century Business Herald , August 7). Huawei’s reaction gave the parody political meaning. Its legal department filed mass complaints with platforms, alleging that the videos used metaphor, homophones, altered audio, and other veiled means to vilify and mock the company and its executives ( 21st Century Business Herald , August 3).  [3] The complaints reminded one commentator of an earlier case, in which a Shanghai media professional wrote a poem about cicadas that his employer judged to be an allusion to Xi. His Weibo post was deleted and his account silenced ( China Digital Times , August 10). The second way in which public pushback occurs is questioning, which targets how Huawei treats ordinary people. In December 2018, Shenzhen police detained former Huawei employee Li Hongyuan (李洪元) after the company reported him. The following August, prosecutors declined to indict him, citing unclear facts and insufficient evidence. He had spent 251 days in custody and later received state compensation. Huawei responded that it “has the right, and also the obligation” (有权利，也有义务) to report suspected illegal conduct to the judicial authorities, adding that it supported him in using legal means to defend his rights and interests, including by suing Huawei ( Yicai , December 2, 2019). One outlet summarized a metaphor then circulating online as “the elephant stamps once, and the ant may stamp back. The rights are the same, the damage vastly different” (大象踩一脚，蚂蚁可回踩。权利相同，杀伤迥异) ( The Cover , December 3, 2019). Censorship turned this labor dispute into a protest against speech controls. Internet users flooded the comments beneath an open letter that Meng had published at the time with the string “985, 996, 251, 404.” The four numbers refer, respectively, to elite university credentials, the work schedule of 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. six days a week, the days Li spent in custody, and the error code displayed when a web page has been deleted. These comments were subsequently removed as well. The New York Times reported that many people in the PRC were especially outraged by the censorship of news coverage and online responses. They said that they had felt helpless at being unable to criticize the government and now felt that they were “also not able to criticize a giant corporation” ( The New York Times , December 4, 2019). The third category of pushback ties Huawei directly to the Party-state. This includes comments such as those posted after the Maextro video was taken down that Huawei had achieved “strong leadership” on the Party’s behalf. On X, one user wrote that blocking and removal across the entire Internet was a concrete expression of “stressing politics” (讲政治), a discipline that the Party requires of cadres and the media ( X/@justicefallen20 , October 9). Another was blunter, asking “whose company is Huawei? If we cannot deal with the red sun, can we at least deal with you, Huawei?” (华为是谁的企业呀？处理不了红太阳，还解决不了你华为吗？) ( X/@Neo_Marici , October 9). The user’s meaning is that those who are powerless against Xi can vent their anger on Huawei. Efforts to Shield Huawei Backfire In the past, and especially after the Meng Wanzhou affair, propagandists could readily turn measures to protect Huawei to their advantage. In June 2019, Shenzhen police acted on a report from Huawei and placed two people in administrative detention for spreading rumors in WeChat groups, among them a claim that Huawei employees had spied for the United States ( Xinhua , June 13, 2019). As the Li Hongyuan case gathered attention, the Global Times asserted that many Internet users had redirected their criticism toward foreign media, believing that the United States was exploiting the case to smear Huawei ( Global Times , December 6, 2019). Today, Huawei more often handles public opinion through legal complaints.  [4] During the bamboo cicada affair, the Harmony Intelligent Mobility Alliance (HIMA; 鸿蒙智行), Huawei’s automotive business, stated on August 4 that it respected normal online expression and well-intentioned criticism. It said that it had filed complaints against only 171 of the more than 56,000 related posts it had monitored, that platforms had removed 144 of them, and that its targets were malicious edits, imitations of executives’ voices, and similar content ( IT Home , August 4). Some bloggers countered that videos that merely showed the toy had also been taken down ( 21st Century Business Herald , August 3). At one point, a Weibo search for “bamboo cicada” came back nearly empty ( Storm Media , August 7). Huawei’s heavy-handed approach backfired. The content it complained about spread more widely. Internet users bought bamboo cicadas to film their own versions, captioned with phrases such as “the lingering sound circles the rafters” (余音绕梁), which plays on the character for Yu’s surname, and “shaking ahead” (摇摇领先), a pun on Yu’s slogan, which was named one of the top ten internet buzzwords of 2023 ( The Paper , December 8, 2023; HK01 , August 3). One outlet called this Huawei’s “Streisand effect,” in which an attempt to suppress information spreads it further ( Storm Media , August 7). As a Caixin commentary argued, the affair had weakened Huawei’s sacred aura in the public mind and brought latent public opinion into the open ( Caixin , August 6). The extent of the backlash became clear when official media ceased to speak with one voice in Huawei’s defense. On August 5, the WeChat account of the Zhejiang Provincial Party Committee’s propaganda department wrote that the stronger a company is, the more open it should be to discussion ( WeChat/Zhejiang Xuanchuan , August 5). A commentary the same day in the official newspaper of the Jiangsu Provincial Party Committee likewise observed that Huawei could hardly avoid giving the impression of overzealous rights protection and of making a fuss over a trifle ( Xinhua Daily , August 5). Provincial propaganda organs had stepped in to urge a company to be magnanimous. The space for criticizing Huawei is evidently far wider than that for criticizing Party and government bodies. The brake incident in October played out as a replay of the bamboo cicada affair. First came efforts to absolve Huawei. Weibo chief executive Wang Gaofei (王高飞) replied to a user that JAC had built the car and that the making of a brake pedal lay outside Huawei’s “empowerment” (赋能) role ( ITHome , October 8). Next came attacks on the tester. Dongchedi’s head of testing said that his phone had been bombarded with text messages ( MyDrivers , October 9). Then the video was taken down, and the target of mockery moved from the brake pedal to censorship. One Weibo user wrote that the takedown merely “hammered nails into Maextro’s coffin lid” (给尊界的棺材板上钉上钉子) ( Weibo , October 9). The official WeChat account of the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region (XUAR) government then published an article criticizing Maextro for evading the question. It drew more than 100,000 views within half a day and was hidden by the account that evening ( Lianhe Zaobao , October 10). Two days later, Zhejiang Xuanchuan weighed in again. It noted that the test video could no longer be viewed on multiple platforms and that many posts discussing it had vanished, and it called the habit of dismissing safety questions as smears against domestic cars an “irrational mentality of shielding one’s own” (非理性的护短心态) ( Zhejiang Xuanchuan , October 12). On October 13, Maextro published a third-party test report stating that the brake pedal met the industry standard, but the testing institution said that the report applied only to the samples the company had submitted and offered no guarantee for vehicles in mass production ( Yicai , October 13). As of this article’s publication, the episode is still unfolding. Conclusion By making Huawei a national symbol, Beijing has allowed the company to become a target of public discontent, deflecting people’s ire from the authorities themselves. Mockery of Huawei uses the same homophones and veiled allusions as mockery of the Party-state. While it also draws complaints and takedowns, it does so at a far lower cost. Huawei is the most prominent firm in Beijing’s narrative of technological self-reliance. As public deference toward it declines, the persuasiveness of that narrative declines with it. The Party may already have realized that the public is magnifying Huawei’s problems as a way of alluding to the Party-state, which is perhaps why central media declined to defend Huawei as they had in 2019. On October 10, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) and three other departments solicited public comment on a draft notice that tightens the management of automotive research, development, testing, and validation ( MIIT , October 10). The next day, the People’s Daily named the Maextro V800 and declared that “a car’s brake pedal should never ‘break’ while driving” (一辆汽车的刹车踏板，绝不应该在驾驶中出现‘断裂’) ( People’s Daily , October 11). Beijing will continue to hold up Huawei as the standard-bearer of high-tech enterprise, but it may keep the company at a greater distance in its propaganda and defend its privileges less conspicuously. Notes [1] The brackets on the three cars broke on the third, fourth, and second stops, respectively. Dongchedi stated that seven other models with plastic pedal brackets completed six stops intact, and it rejected the charge that it had conducted “violent testing” (暴力测试) ( ITHome , October 8). [2] “Teacher Li Is Not Your Teacher” (@whyyoutouzhele) is run by Li Ying (李颖), a Chinese artist based in Italy who has long compiled submissions and comments from internet users inside the PRC. X is blocked in the PRC. The X users cited here are most likely overseas or using circumvention tools, and both their identities and those of the users who submitted comments remain unverified. [3] Homophones and veiled allusion are also the techniques that PRC internet users commonly employ to evade censorship and discuss sensitive political topics. Such expression resembles what James C. Scott called the “hidden transcript” of the weak, in which discontent is voiced through rumor, ambiguity, and jokes. See James C. Scott, Domination and the Arts of Resistance: Hidden Transcripts (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1990). [4] Other large firms also use legal means against critics. In June 2025, BYD said that it was suing 37 “smear accounts” (黑号) and had placed another 126 accounts on a watch list ( Jiemian News , June 4, 2025). The post Huawei Becomes Proxy for Public Criticism of Party-State appeared first on Jamestown .

title: Temple Management and Potential Pathways for Corruption in Taiwan
zh_title: 台湾寺庙管理与腐败潜在途径
source: 华盛顿全球台湾研究中心
summary: 封面图片：台湾大溪镇的庙会（2013 年 8 月 1 日）。无意暗示该寺庙或附属组织参与任何非法活动。台湾最神圣的道教药神的庙宇保生大帝位于台南薛家。该寺庙由当地一位有权有势的人物王文宗管理，王文宗在中文中的意思是“杰出作家”。王的名字，以及保生大地的治疗作用，与王的个人历史形成鲜明对比。 2022 年，王涉嫌策划了一场枪击事件，期间有人持枪
content:
封面图片：台湾大溪镇的庙会（2013 年 8 月 1 日）。无意暗示该寺庙或附属组织参与任何非法活动。台湾最神圣的道教药神的庙宇保生大帝位于台南薛家。该寺庙由当地一位有权有势的人物王文宗管理，王文宗在中文中的意思是“杰出作家”。王的名字，以及保生大地的治疗作用，与王的个人历史形成鲜明对比。据称，2022 年，王某策划了一场枪击事件，一名枪手向与台湾民进党结盟的政客拥有的两处房产倾倒了 88 颗子弹。王是该阴谋的著名策划者，他支付了枪手及其同伙逃往中华人民共和国（中国）福建省的相关费用。王甚至两次前往中国会见同谋，支付后者的酒店房间费用，并允许该男子使用自己的身份使用中国支付应用程序。王于 2023 年 3 月被捕，检察官提供了他参与犯罪的证据。然而，2023 年 12 月，即王因试图逃离该国而被捕八个月后，他再次当选为供奉治愈之神的学家神社慈济宫的院长。
此案引发了人们对台湾寺庙治理和基层社会的好奇：一个安排冲锋枪袭击两名政客财产的人如何仍然是台湾著名寺庙的领导人？2024年2月，王文宗因窝藏罪被判入狱六个月。截至2026年10月，他仍在领导薛家的寺庙活动，向信徒分发现金礼物，并带领游行庆祝保生大地。为什么一个有能力组织如此耸人听闻的犯罪事件的人会对管理道观感兴趣呢？寺庙是台湾草根传统社会中具有深远影响的机构，这种社区在台北或新竹等城市化、受过高等教育的地区之外广泛存在。由于寺庙是居民的社区聚会点，并且是向当地公民分配赞助的允许渠道，因此寻求政治权力的犯罪分子有很强的动机来接管寺庙的管理。大多数台湾寺庙很可能不受帮派控制；然而，台湾有许多著名的寺庙是由被指控的有组织犯罪头目经营的。寺庙是帮派头目的有吸引力的控制目标，因为几乎没有任何法规要求向台湾政府提供详细的财务报告。
寺庙的财务和人事管理受到一套内部规则的约束，这些规则的稳健性决定了犯罪分子对相关寺庙建立控制的容易程度。寺庙也是犯罪分子与地方和国家政客建立关系的有效渠道，因为民选官员会被寺庙举办的众多活动以及随后与当地选民建立联系的机会所吸引。本文基于对台湾政府官员、学者和寺庙管理人员的采访，揭示了导致所谓帮派头目和寺庙马之间存在明显重叠的系统。

【原文 English Original】
Cover image: A temple festival in Ta Hsi Township (大溪鎮), Taiwan (August 1, 2013). No implication is intended that this temple or affiliated organizations is involved with any illegal activities. Taiwan’s most holy temple to the Daoist medicine god, Baosheng Dadi (保生大帝), is found in Xuejia, Tainan. The temple is managed by a powerful local figure named Wang Wen-tsung (王文宗), a name that means “eminent writer” in literary Chinese. Wang’s name, as well as the therapeutic role of Baosheng Dadi, contrast with Wang’s personal history. In 2022, Wang allegedly orchestrated a shooting during which a gunman unloaded 88 bullets into two properties owned by politicians aligned with Taiwan’s Democratic Progressive Party (民進黨). Wang was the reputed mastermind behind the plot, paying for expenses related to the gunman and an accomplice’s escape to Fujian Province, in the People’s Republic of China (PRC). Wang even travelled twice to meet the accomplice in China, paying for the latter’s hotel rooms and allowing the man to use his identity for Chinese payment apps. Wang was arrested in March 2023, and prosecutors laid out the evidence for his involvement with the crime. Yet in December 2023, eight months after Wang had been arrested trying to flee the country, he was re-elected as chairman of Ciji Temple (慈濟宮), the Xuejia shrine dedicated to the god of healing. This case raises curious questions about Taiwan’s temple governance and grassroots society: How can a man who arranged for a submachine gun attack on two politicians’ properties remain the leader of an eminent temple in Taiwan? In February 2024, Wang Wen-tsung was convicted of harboring a criminal and sentenced to six months in prison. As of October 2026, he was still leading temple events in Xuejia, distributing cash gifts to worshippers, and leading processions in celebration of Baosheng Dadi. Why would someone capable of organizing such a sensational crime take an interest in managing a Daoist temple in the first place? Temples are deeply influential institutions within Taiwan’s grassroots, traditional society—the kind of communities found widely outside of urbanized, highly-educated locations such as Taipei or Hsinchu. Because temples serve as a community meeting point for residents, and are permissible channels through which patronage can be distributed to local citizens, there is a strong incentive for criminal actors seeking political power to take over management of them. The majority of Taiwanese temples are most likely not gang controlled; however, there are a number of highly prominent temples in Taiwan that are run by alleged organized crime leaders. Temples are attractive targets for control by gang leaders, as there are few to no regulations requiring detailed financial reporting to the Taiwanese government. The financial and personnel management of temples is governed by a set of internal rules, the robustness of which determines how easily criminal actors can establish control over the temples in question. Temples are also effective conduits through which criminal figures can establish relationships with local and national politicians, as elected officials are drawn to the well-attended events thrown by temples and the subsequent opportunities to connect with local voters. Based on interviews with Taiwanese government officials, scholars, and temple managers, this article unpacks the system that has produced a conspicuous degree of overlap between alleged gang leaders and temple managers. Government Regulation in Name Only Because Taiwanese temples predate the development of Taiwan’s modern legal system, the institutions are afforded a special place in Taiwanese regulation. In an interview, Howard Wu (吳浩遠) of the Tainan City Civil Affairs Bureau (民政局)—the local government department that oversees temples—shared with me that unlike Christian churches, temples are not required to establish foundations to operate. Indeed, there are few direct regulations that can compel a temple operator to register their temple at all. In other words, an individual can start a Daoist temple or shrine in their home, accept cash donations, and spend those cash donations in any way they see fit without breaking the law. [1] In a separate interview, a senior official in Taiwan’s Ministry of the Interior (內政部) shared that as long as the operator of the shrine restricted individual transactions to under NTD 500,000 (USD 15,650), they could conceivably funnel cash donations to their personal accounts and escape the notice of banks’ anti-money laundering systems. [2] Yet even if a temple registers with its local civil affairs bureau, the requirements for financial reporting are extremely lax. Wu pointed out that a temple must submit a biannual financial report that shares topline figures for the money received in donations, and the money spent by the temple. The financial administrator of the temple need not provide any proof for the reported figures, nor must they itemize revenues or expenses. Over a banquet dinner (辦桌), the financial administrator of a Tainan temple dedicated to the City God (城隍爺) cheerfully told me that “it is a very simple system.” [3] Wu, the Tainan City official, admitted that the government cannot impose penalties on temples even for non-compliance with these simple financial reporting requirements. Instead, local governments rely on inducements to encourage temple managers to adhere to rules. Wu outlined that any temple with an ambition to attract substantial donations will register with local authorities, as registration confers a sense of legitimacy that worshippers reward with cash contributions. Registered temples are also able to issue receipts through which donors can apply for tax deductions. Yet in order to incentivize temples to comply with even the meager reporting requirements conferred by Taiwanese law, local authorities dole out subsidies for temple events—and, in the case of particularly historical temples, money for building improvements. Perhaps more importantly than the superficial financial reporting requirements, temple registration calls for managers to disclose the institution’s organizational chart, which may change at each temple election. This is important for local officials, as it allows them to understand whether a temple is adhering to its own bylaws for managing leadership, or whether a few individuals have established corrupt control over the temple’s administration. Local governments will occasionally raise objections if they find that a temple has not adhered to its personnel management bylaws. Ultimately, however, whether or not temple managers abuse the political and financial power of temples is less a product of government regulation, and more the outcome of the internal governance systems of each institution. Indeed, as the financial administrator of the City God temple in Tainan conceded to me: “[T]he temple manager has the power to decide most of what we do.” The Internal Governance Systems of Temples No two temples operate identical internal governance systems. These systems generally reflect decisions made at the time of the temple’s founding, and the communities around the temple. Most temples are organized by a committee (委員會), and occasionally by “boards” (董事會)—if they have established foundations or simply wish to adopt that nomenclature to present a more official image. Committees and boards will include individuals that have taken on specific roles, such as chair (主委, 董事長), vice chair (副主委, 副董事長), supervisor (常務監事), and financial administrator (財務委員). Internal practices, such as accounting, are determined by committee members—and may be concentrated under the authority of the chair, or shared among multiple officials. The City God temple financial administrator described a robust system to me. Boxes containing cash donations are opened monthly by a group of no fewer than three people. Donations are counted collectively and deposited to an account held under the names of two officials. Meanwhile, any expense over NTD 1000 (approximately USD 31) must be reported to the temple committee. (The itemized expenses were not shared with the local government.) However, the financial administrator pointed out that in other temples, bookkeeping may be purely executed by the temple chair, who is often the only full-time official in the institution. Image: Joss paper (金紙) stacked on shelves in a Taiwanese temple. Devotees exchange cash donations (香油錢) for joss paper and burn it to honor gods or ancestors. (Image Source: Boattoad, Wikimedia Commons ) It is in the election process for the committee chairs, who manage the institution, that temples demonstrate either resilience or susceptibility to corrupt leadership. Dr. Sher Chien-Yuan (佘健源), professor at National Sun Yat-sen University (國立中山大學) in Kaohsiung, classifies temples into two broad buckets: “new” and “old” temples. Old temples find their roots in Han communities that originally settled in various parts of Taiwan. New temples may have been constructed by internal migrants in Taiwan, or recently by businesspeople wishing to leave a physical representation of their legacies. Old temples often have highly restrictive eligibility criteria for membership. Charles Chang (張瑞麟), a committee member of Ji Dian Wu Miao (祀典武廟), a temple in Tainan that receives government funding due to its historical status, underscored to me that only direct descendants of the original families that founded the temple could serve as committee members. These committee members would elect the chair who manages the temple. There were 110 spots available in the committee, and an applicant would have to wait until an existing member passed away before they could join. His daughters had been waiting in line to join the committee for many years. [4] Indeed, I interviewed committee members at multiple temples who described extended waiting periods for membership, sometimes stretching decades. One interviewee belonging to a prominent Mazu (媽祖) temple in Kaohsiung outlined an even stricter system. The temple had been built by three villages, and so direct descendants of the original inhabitants of each village were permitted to gather periodically and elect 21 representatives. The 21 representatives of each village would then elect 21 members among them to serve on the temple committee. Finally, the 21 committee members would choose the chair. [5] In theory, highly restrictive election systems such as these would hamper the ability of corrupt or criminal actors to gain leadership over temples. One member of an old temple in Tainan told me the committee would pay careful attention to the backgrounds of applicants, and would not admit a member who had a suspect past. [6] However, as Dr. Sher explained to me, certain “new” temples have been constructed more recently by internal migrant communities, such as those who arrived in Kaohsiung during its industrialization boom in the 1970s. These migrant communities were naturally more transient, and could not ground committee membership in historical ties to a particular area. Membership might be more open—or, in the case of new temples struggling to attract donations, welcoming to businesspeople able to provide resources to grow the assets of the temple. [7] One academic survey found that when choosing which temples to visit, Taiwanese worshippers are particularly sensitive to the perceived financial health of the institution: the better the financial health of the temple, the more visitors it receives and the greater the donation figures. In this context, gang leaders—who almost always own legitimate businesses through which to disguise their wealth—can be seen as worthy investors in temples, capable of drawing more devotees through bigger processions or improved physical premises. In a remarkable set of structured interviews with gang members in Taiwan, a Ministry of Interior Criminal Investigation Bureau (刑事警察局) official, Yueh Ying-Chung (岳瀛宗), learned that some gangsters regard temples as businesses to be developed. Recounting the growth of one temple, a gangster stated, “It was originally just a small altar, but later, as the incense offerings grew, it gradually expanded. The donations from believers were substantial, and training the procession was also a matter of prestige, which helped increase income.” Indeed, the gangsters interviewed by Yueh were particularly drawn to the revenue-generating power of temples: “For temples of any size, annual donations from believers are often tens of millions, and some believers’ donations for fulfilling vows are even more lavish.” Charles Chang, the committee member of Ji Dian Wu Miao in Tainan—a temple that does not have gang connections—told me that donations to his temple had reached NTD 50 million (USD 1.6 million) last year. [8] Whether by founding new shrines, offering their financial clout to struggling temples, or simply buying existing ones (since the assets owned by a temple are transferrable), criminal actors are able to secure a greater degree of control over temples with weak internal management systems. Once in control of a given temple, a corrupt or criminal actor can seek to use its resources and convening power to foster alliances with politicians: for example, in order to win bidding processes for government contracts. Speaking of the usefulness of temples for gangs that run construction businesses and compete for government tenders, a gangster interviewed by Yueh Ying-Chung stated: If the temple is big enough, and is very famous with a large following, high officials, even presidents will come to visit. This changes its image, and donations will be substantial. So it’s easier for these companies to introduce bids or change government procurement offers, business will be easier, and lower officials won’t come and cause trouble. A criminal actor in charge of a temple could also use their position to enlarge religious exchanges with Daoist shrines in the PRC, activity that the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) has long promoted as part of its united front political warfare strategy directed at Taiwan. The Chinese Unification Promotion Party (中華統一促進黨), a sham political party in Taiwan founded by gang members, has—according to a Ministry of Interior senior official—purchased more than a dozen temples and is using them to promote a pro-unification agenda allegedly financed by the CCP. Even for so-called “old” temples, the pull of enormous donation receipts has encouraged some corrupt actors to seek control over management. This is especially true for temples to Mazu, a sea goddess that has achieved enormous popular appeal due to several massive pilgrimages organized in Taiwan each year. The vice chair of the eminent Mazu temple in Kaohsiung told me that all around the island, elections for chairs of Mazu temples had been growing more competitive. Despite the extremely restricted membership process for his temple—allowing eligibility for descendants of just three villages—the vice chair confided that committee members had recently convened to vote out a chair who had been diverting donation revenues to friends acting as vendors to the temple. [9] Since large temples employ part-time workers, source supplies such as joss paper (金紙) from sellers, and conduct frequent building maintenance and improvements, it was possible for the corrupt former chair to funnel revenues to cronies who had asked for a share of the temple’s vast donations. The committee voted the corrupt chair out only narrowly. This incident illustrates that temples with more robust internal governance systems are better equipped to resist unscrupulous management—but that even older and well-established temples in Taiwan can become the targets of corrupt control. Image: A traditional Taiwanese street banquet (辦桌) in Tainan attended by the author. A number of politicians competing for local office attended this annual celebration, organized by a City God temple. (Image Source: Author’s photograph) The Draw of the Political Power of Temples How, in particular, can temples afford criminal actors political power? In Taiwan’s democratic era of competitive elections, the ability of temples to convene local residents has rendered them critical outreach targets for politicians. Some 60 percent of Taiwanese citizens observe some kind of deity worship. And since devotees to Daoist temples are typically concentrated among older populations , temples and the elaborate events that they hold afford politicians a chance to connect with reliable voters. As one election researcher at the National Chengchi University (國立政治大學) put it : “Everyone’s going to temples, if you don’t, you fall behind.” During the 2024 presidential election, the three major candidates made over 400 visits to temples (of which nearly 30 percent were Mazu temples). The benefit to temples of high-level visits by politicians has been articulated by the gang members interviewed by Yueh of the Criminal Investigation Bureau: “Once a temple gains scale and reputation, politicians will flock to worship it, further elevating its religious status and fame.” But, what are the precise ways that a temple can help a particular candidate during an election? There was once a time, in the early years of Taiwan’s democracy, that a temple might issue open support for a particular candidate. For example, in 2000, Jenn Lann Temple, one of the most prominent Mazu shrines in central Taiwan, held a divination that found that their Mazu preferred the candidate James Soong (宋楚瑜) for the presidency. However, temples have moved beyond this degree of overt support for a particular candidate, partly because the strategy is risky: in that case, Soong lost the election, leaving Jenn Lann Temple to engage with a president it had not supported. Instead, Dr. Ku Ming-Chun (古明君), professor at Tsinghua University in Hsinchu, told me that temples’ support for candidates will be more “subtle.” When throwing elaborate processions, such as Jenn Lann Temple’s Dajia Mazu pilgrimage (大甲媽祖遶境) that draws millions of attendees each year, a temple will invite candidates from all parties. However, the temple management may afford a favorite candidate a more advantageous position in the proceedings, such as when the goddess statue originally departs her mother temple in front of heaving crowds. Ku noted that temples may also offer politicians honorary titles, such as an “advisor” (顧問), which the politician can flaunt in order to curry favor with a given area’s voters. [10] Image: Temple volunteers distribute free bread to devotees during the Baishatun (白沙屯) Mazu pilgrimage in 2018 (Image Source: Wikimedia commons ) However, perhaps the most important resource that temples can lend politicians is the grassroots influence of the chairs themselves. Because temple chairs ostensibly command the activities of the temple, and in particular the charity that the temple distributes to local residents, chairs have cultivated deep wells of favor among local residents. In addition to gaudy events designed to entertain local populations, wealthy temples will distribute charity to devotees in the forms of cash-filled “red envelopes” (紅包), food staples such as rice, or scholarships for educational advancement. The favor earned from this activity is no doubt part of the reason that temple chairs with known criminal backgrounds, such as Yen Ching-piao (顏清標), chair of Jenn Lann Temple, or even Wang Wen-tsung of Xuejia Ciji Temple, have been able to hold on to their chairmanship positions. As one former senior Ministry of Interior official told me, when elections roll around, these temple leaders have established such a strong position of local support that their personal political preferences can influence significant numbers of local voters to break for candidates. [11] Some temple chairs can even promise candidates specific numbers of votes when election time rolls around. Yet for temple managers, the surest guarantee of political power is to run for office oneself, or to arrange for family members to run for positions of power. A number of temple chairs hold, or have held, political positions themselves. Examples include Yen Ching-piao (顏清標), who was a Kuomintang (國民黨)-aligned national legislator from 2002 to 2012 ; or Huang Cheng-kuo (黃承國), the chair of Zhinan Temple (指南宮) in Taipei, who was both a gangster and a member of the Central Standing Committee of the Democratic Progressive Party (民進黨). Still more temple chairs have supported family members entering elected politics: such as Tsai Yung-te (蔡咏鍀), chair of Beigang Chaotian Temple ( 北港朝天 宮) , who has allegedly channeled temple funds to a foundation run by his sister, who is a national legislator for the TPP. Even Wang Wen-tsung, the Xuejia Ciji Temple chair who served six months for arranging a shooting attack, can boast of a daughter presently running for city government in Tainan. The main point: While most temples in Taiwan have likely resisted the influence of organized crime, some prominent temples are run by individuals with criminal records and alleged gang leadership roles. Temples enjoy extremely lax regulation in Taiwan, meaning that unscrupulous actors can potentially employ them to funnel worshippers’ donations to cronies, or as conduits for money laundering. Ultimately, internal governance systems determine how easily a temple can be corrupted, and the charity benefits that temples dispense to devotee communities affords temple chairs tremendous levels of political clout. # 中共間諜涉嫌冒充澳退休警察 誘澳人泄露情報

[![Image 4](https://i.epochtimes.com/assets/uploads/2024/10/id14361137-shutterstock_1007210323-600x400.jpg)](https://i.epochtimes.com/assets/uploads/2024/10/id14361137-shutterstock_1007210323-600x400.jpg)

澳洲廣播公司的一項調查發現，一個涉嫌從事間諜活動的中共間諜網絡，利用一家虛構的安保公司，涉嫌冒充澳洲退休警察，將目標對準澳洲人，誘騙他們分享情報。（Shutterstock）

【大紀元2026年10月16日訊】（大紀元記者陳光澳洲悉尼編譯報導）澳洲廣播公司（ABC）的一項調查發現，一個涉嫌從事間諜活動的中共間諜網絡，利用一家虛構的安保公司，據稱由三名澳洲退休警察組成，將目標對準澳洲人，誘騙他們分享情報。

澳洲廣播公司報導說，2020年5月，澳洲律師亨利（Henry，化名）在其社交媒體領英（LinkedIn）上收到了一份非正式的聘用邀請。

「我們正在尋找來自澳洲和加拿大的安全專家顧問（兼職），」一位名叫「Sophy」的人寫道。

該帳戶聲稱自己代表Data 31——一家由三名退休的澳洲警察組織運營的安保諮詢公司，總部位於上海。

亨利是一名擁有美國執業資格、在中國事務方面擁有豐富經驗的律師，其業務涵蓋白領犯罪辯護及相關調查工作。他也曾在澳洲陸軍服役近20年，退役時軍銜為少校。

澳廣的調查現已確認，「Sophy」是一個涉嫌從事間諜活動的中共間諜網絡所使用的多個虛假身分之一，該網絡在2016年至2025年間將全球數千人作為從事間諜活動的目標，其中包括利用Data 31這類虛構公司。

被這些涉嫌中共間諜所接觸的對象包括與澳洲、美國、英國、加拿大和新西蘭（「五眼」情報聯盟成員國）有關聯的政府官員、前軍方人員和安保專家。

2020年，至少有七名澳洲人被名為Data 31的帳戶聯繫過，其中包括有澳洲軍方背景的人士、自由撰稿人和播客主持人、律師、安保主管和澳洲貿易部門代表。

Data 31帳戶在向一位澳洲安保主管發送的消息中稱，他們正在尋找顧問，以開展「積極調查」並撰寫「安全報告」，以「協助上海的銀行、數據公司和風險投資機構」。

但擬議的報告內容卻要求涵蓋國際關係、經濟和反恐等多個領域。

澳廣聯繫了亨利徵求意見，但未收到回復。

澳廣表示，調查尚未發現任何證據表明這些澳洲人接受了撰寫報告的邀請。

這些帳戶擁有跨度超過八年的領英消息記錄。

在過去幾週裡，澳廣審閱了涉嫌與中共間諜活動有關的兩個領英帳戶中的數千條消息。

其中一個帳戶早在 2016 年就已處於活躍狀態。在接下來的幾年裡，他們與數千名用戶建立了聯繫，其中包括澳洲人和曾在澳洲工作過的人。

這些帳號曾聲稱隸屬於多個機構，包括中共政府的旅遊項目、電子公司、電動車品牌、Data31以及另外兩個虛構的中國智庫。它們還使用過多個化名，包括「Sophy Ding」、「Hanna Lee」和「Vera Su」。

中共間諜的威脅一直是澳洲安全情報局（ASIO）局長伯傑斯（_Mike Burgess_）反覆強調的議題。

情報局在其《2024年年度威脅評估報告》中曾描述了一個中共情報組織「A團隊」的間諜活動，稱該團隊採用了「Sophy」等名字，並聲稱代表 Data 31等虛構公司。

在《2026年年度威脅評估報告》中，安全情報局還透露，一名外國間諜冒充顧問，在網上聯繫了一名持有澳洲安全許可的人員。

伯傑斯說，該名間諜付錢給這位官員，讓他寫兩份關於澳洲與太平洋鄰國關係的報告，並認為他已被拉下水，又出錢要求對方提供有關澳英美聯盟（AUKUS）的內部情報。

該官員起了疑心，並將此事報告給了澳洲安全情報局。

title: 监控录下中国女留学生投毒同窗关键画面，其于机场入境前被控
source: 澳洲唐人街 – Australia ChinaTown News 中文华人新闻
summary: 10月6日，32岁的中国籍博士生Aili Wang在洛杉矶国际机场被捕。 据美联社报道，她涉嫌在怀俄明大学（University of Wyoming）同一间办公室的同学的茶水中下毒。 受害者是怀俄明大学的一名越南籍研究生，法庭文件中只称他为“K.T.”。 两人的导师、微生物学教授Mark Gomelsky形容他是一名非常出色的学生。 K.T.的研究方向是利用细菌把RNA输送进人体细胞，这项研究由美国联邦政府资助，已经申请了专利，涉及癌症、神经系统疾病和遗传病治疗的新技术。
content: 10月6日，32岁的中国籍博士生Aili Wang在洛杉矶国际机场被捕。 据美联社报道，她涉嫌在怀俄明大学（University of Wyoming）同一间办公室的同学的茶水中下毒。 受害者是怀俄明大学的一名越南籍研究生，法庭文件中只称他为“K.T.”。 两人的导师、微生物学教授Mark Gomelsky形容他是一名非常出色的学生。 K.T.的研究方向是利用细菌把RNA输送进人体细胞，这项研究由美国联邦政府资助，已经申请了专利，涉及癌症、神经系统疾病和遗传病治疗的新技术。 今年8月，K.T.参加了一场重要的学术会议。 回来后不久，他就开始出现奇怪的症状：极度疲惫、失眠，手指刺痛麻木，双腿无力。 他还发现，自己用办公桌上的小咖啡机泡的茶，有一股怪味。 每次把咖啡机洗干净，怪味就会消失一阵。 Gomelsky开始怀疑，同一间办公室里有人在给他下毒。 K.T.的妻子和其他几个人决定自己查。他们把办公室咖啡机里的水煮干，得到了63毫克白色粉末。 一位化学教授检测后确认，这是丙烯酰胺。 丙烯酰胺最广为人知的是作为淀粉类食物高温烹饪、以及烟草燃烧时产生的致癌副产物。 高剂量时具有急性毒性，在微生物学研究中常被用于蛋白质或DNA实验。 参与检测的助理教授Tak Sumaya说，一发现是这种物质，他就立刻起了疑心，因为在那种地方不可能自然出现这么多丙烯酰胺。 他们把样本交给了校园警察。 监控拍下翻桌子、拍笔记 随后，K.T.和校园警察在他与Aili Wang共用的办公室里装了监控。 据校园警察的宣誓书，9月27日，监控拍到Aili Wang在翻K.T.的书桌。 10月1日，她又被拍到在K.T.桌上拍照、翻动笔记本，还用她自己杯子里的液体冲洗K.T.的杯子。 Sumaya说，她把K.T.留在桌上的一本笔记本每一页都拍了下来。 宣誓书指出，两人研究领域不同，关系也一直不好，Aili Wang没有任何理由去翻K.T.的书桌。 而她来美国之前，据称在中国做过类似的研究。 导师Gomelsky透露，Aili Wang第一次博士论文答辩没有通过，对K.T.的研究成果心生嫉妒。 从今年6月起，她就没再做实验，一直在写论文。 问话第二天，现身机场 10月5日，校园警察找Aili Wang问话。 据称，她表示自己已经好几年没用过丙烯酰胺了。 第二天，她就在洛杉矶国际机场被捕。警方称，她当时正准备返回中国。 警方还调查发现，她去年夏天曾两次在eBay上购买丙烯酰胺，之后还要求eBay删除她的账户。 Aili Wang被控一项重罪：加重攻击和殴打罪，最高可判10年监禁，并处1万美元（约1.78万纽币）罚款。 她原本的保释金是20万美元（约35.6万纽币）。 怀俄明州检方以她有逃跑风险为由，申请大幅提高保释金。 当地法官同意了这一请求，把保释金提高到150万美元（约267万纽币），且只接受现金。 目前还不清楚她何时会被引渡回怀俄明州受审。法庭文件中没有列出她的代理律师，美联社也没能联系上她本人。 多年来，美国官员一直指控中国从美国大学窃取知识产权。 不过，目前Aili Wang面临的指控只涉及下毒，以上均为指控，尚未经法庭定罪。 Gomelsky说，K.T.至今仍有中毒症状。 他告诉美联社，看着自己一个学生生命受到威胁，而另一个学生可能就是加害者，这是他职业生涯中最震惊的经历之一。 这起案件在Reddit新闻版块r/news引发热议，相关帖子获得了2600多个赞。 点赞最高的一条评论只有一句话：等等，又一个华人投毒者？ 类似的事，并不是第一次发生。 华人工程师给同胞投毒 据美国ABC7电视台报道，10月12日，加州伯克利（Berkeley）一名法官批准了一名华人男子David Xu清除重罪记录的申请，而他曾被定罪给同事下毒。 受害者Rong Yuan是一名工程师。 从2017年起，她开始出现呕吐、脱发等不明原因的健康问题，两年多里看了无数医生，病情却越来越重。 转机来自她的母亲。母亲发现她的水杯有一股怪味，洗了也没用。 Rong Yuan于是在自己办公桌上装了一个小摄像头。 摄像头拍到，她的同事David Xu往她的水杯里倒东西。 检测发现，那是有毒的重金属镉。 报道称，水样中的镉含量是美国联邦标准的350万倍。 由于家里做饭也用过这个水杯里的水，Rong Yuan和父母三人都检出了镉中毒。 2019年，David Xu被控蓄意谋杀未遂。 但2023年，他与检方达成认罪协议，承认投毒罪，只被判了两年缓刑，没有额外的监禁。 缓刑期满后，他向法院申请撤销定罪。阿拉米达县检察官办公室和受害者一起表示反对，但法官仍然批准了。 Rong Yuan至今不知道对方为什么要害她。 她的父亲去年因心力衰竭去世。 她说，自己一直很内疚：如果当初没让父母来美国，如果没把那瓶水带回家，他们就不会中毒。 将近十年过去，她的身体仍未恢复，只能做兼职工作。她曾申请50万美元赔偿，最终只拿到7000美元。 2023年，美国南佛罗里达大学36岁的中国籍化学博士生Li Xuming，因为嫌楼上邻居家太吵，把矛头指向了邻居刚出生的女儿。 当年5月底到6月底，他至少三次用注射器，把美沙酮和氢可酮的混合药物注射进邻居家门缝。 邻居一家三口反复出现呼吸困难、眼睛和皮肤不适等症状。 起初，Li Xuming和邻居关系还不错，他甚至在孩子出生后送过一条小裙子。后来他开始频繁发短信抱怨噪音，邻居却觉得那些噪音根本不存在。 邻居起了疑心，在门外装了隐蔽摄像头。 2023年6月27日傍晚，摄像头拍下了他再次作案的画面，他当晚被捕。 Li Xuming被控殴打、散布化学制剂和持有管制药物等罪名，随后被学校开除，2023年底被遣返回中国。 投毒是犯罪，没有任何借口。 但案件背后那些被忽视的信号：学术圈的高压、心理支持的缺失、人际关系的恶化。 如果没有人去正视，下一个“Aili Wang”可能已经在某个实验室里悄悄买好了化学品。 投毒是犯罪，没有任何借口。 但案件背后那些被忽视的信号：学术圈的高压、心理支持的缺失、人际关系的恶化。 如果没有人去正视，下一个“Aili Wang”可能已经在某个实验室里悄悄买好了化学品。

content: 【大纪元2026年10月15日讯】今年5月、9月，美国总统川普和中共党魁习近平实现了互访。两次“川习会”后，国际上对美台关系议论纷纷。尽管两次“川习会”上，习近平都跟川普谈了台湾问题，但是，并没有改变美国政府对台湾的立场。相反，美台关系持续全面升级，至少有六大进展。 一、美台关系全面升级的六大进展 第一，台湾对美国5000 亿美元的投资承诺在兑现中。 川普总统第二任期开始后，据美国官方数据，台湾对美国承诺的投资总额已达5000亿美元。 7月16日，美国商务部宣布：台积电将在美国亚利桑那州追加1,000亿美元投资，用于生产先进半导体及封装设备。加上此前的投资承诺，台积电在美投资总额将达到2,650亿美元，规划厂区增至12座，成为美国历史上规模最大的外来直接投资。 美国商务部的声明称，台积电的新增投资将给美国带来数以万计的就业机会，将先进半导体的制造带回美国，并带动数十亿美元的间接经济产出。 美国在台协会（AIT）处长谷立言（Raymond F. Greene）说，这项投资“充分展现美国与台湾对彼此的信任与信心，而这正是美台伙伴关系的核心”。 第二，台湾购买美国液化天然气被称为“史上最大的交易之一”。 川普在阿拉斯加瓦西拉的集会上宣布：台湾已同意在未来20年内购买阿拉斯加液化天然气管道项目约30%的产量。据路透社报导，川普称这直接保证了该项目的彻底成功，也是史上最大的交易之一。 10月14日，台湾经济部证实，台湾“中油股份有限公司”已于2025年3月签署买卖暨投资意向书，历经近一年半协商后取得重大进展。规划内容包括项目投产后每年采购600万吨液化天然气，并参与项目开发，投资金额最高44亿美元，最快2032年起供气。 台湾经济部强调，该项目可经太平洋航线直达台湾，有助于分散运输路线与地缘供应风险。 第三，美国企业加大对台湾的投资力度。 10月8日，美国总统川普在华盛顿举行的“科学：新黄金时代”峰会上，向6位科技界领袖颁发了美国科学与技术领域的最高国家荣誉。 其中，两位出生于台湾的美国科技巨头——英伟达创始人兼首席执行官黄仁勋，超微半导体董事长兼首席执行官苏姿丰，获颁“国家科学奖章”。 黄仁勋的英伟达、苏姿丰的超微，与台湾AI产业有千丝万缕的联系。 英伟达绝大部分的高端图形处理器与人工智能芯片，都交由台湾的台积电进行独家或主要代工生产。英伟达在台湾的合作伙伴还包括鸿海、广达、纬创、华硕、微星、技嘉等。 5月27日，黄仁勋在台北宣布：英伟达将在台湾建立总部并扩大投资，每年预估投入约1500亿美元。 超微半导体在台湾的合作伙伴包括台积电、日月光、硅品、力成、欣兴、景硕、纬创、纬颖、英业达、台达电、营邦等。 5月21日，苏姿丰宣布：超微将在台湾AI产业投资超过100亿美元，用于加速建置AI基础设施与提升先进封装产能。 10月6日，苏姿丰再度访台时表示，由于AI市场需求暴增，相关投资计划进展顺利并决定继续调高投资金额。 谷歌、苹果、微软等美国的科技巨头，都在台湾供应链中深度布局。 比如，谷歌在台湾设立了美国总部以外全球最大的硬件与AI基础建设研发中心。苹果在台湾设有研发中心和技术实验室，且其全球有四分之一的供应链厂商位于台湾。微软在台湾设有数据中心与亚洲首座AI研发中心。这些美国科技巨头都在台湾持续投资。 第四，台美在无人机方面的合作取得新突破。 俄乌战争使无人机在现代战争中的作用变得异常关键。受乌克兰的启发，台湾在无人机方面也迅速赶上。 台湾从2022年起启动无人机计划。台湾无人机的产量从2024年的约1万架增加到2025年的超过12万架，并计划到2028年年产18万架。 美国国防科技公司安杜里尔（Anduril）创办人拉奇（Palmer Luckey）在一个国际论坛上说，面对地缘政治挑战，台湾建构不对称作战能力的进展速度，“比我们合作的绝大多数国家都快得多，其中也包括美国”。 台积电被称为台湾的“护国神山”。台湾正在迅速崛起的无人机产业群，有望成为台湾的又一座“护国神山”。 美台在无人机方面的合作，从天空到水面，从短程到远程，从“美国设计，台湾制造”到“共同设计，台湾制造”，正全方位展开。 10月13日，《华尔街日报》报导，在与台湾合作开发海空无人机的美国业者中，安杜里尔对台无人机合约已逾10亿美元。 同日，美国国防科技公司Shield AI正式宣布：已与台湾合作伙伴汉翔航空工业共同完成首架V-BAT垂直起降监侦无人机的设计、生产、组装、测试；该无人机已运抵台湾海巡署。未来数月内，将陆续交付12架V-BAT给台湾海巡署。 V-BAT属于第三级（Group 3）无人飞行系统，采用涵道风扇设计，并搭载重油引擎，主要用于情报、监视与侦察，以及目标锁定等任务。 10月2日，美国国防科技企业AEVEX的成长策略资深副总裁安德斯（Craig Anders）宣布：将与台湾中光电智能机器人公司合作生产VANDAL与ONYX两款无人机。不久前这两款无人机已在台东太麻里进行过实际飞行展示。另外，由AEVEX生产的LYNX无人船已由美方交给台湾的海军陆战队操作。 9月中旬，台湾最大造船企业“台湾国际造船股份有限公司”宣布：与美国国防科技公司Havoc AI建立合作伙伴关系，共同推动自主无人水面载具在台湾的生产、技术合作与维护保养。 据美国军事媒体Defense News报导，传统上是美国出口武器给台湾，但在无人机领域，未来可能出现相反方向。 第五，台湾对美国的出口大幅增长。 至2026年9月，台湾出口连续35个月正成长，写下史上最长成长周期。据台湾财政部的数据，台湾9月出口872.2亿美元，年增60.9%，创历年单月新高；累计前9月出口达6615.5亿美元，年增46.2%；全年出口值有望达到9000亿美元。 1—9月，台湾对美国出口总额达到2077.8亿美元，史上首次在同期突破2000亿美元大关，提前刷新了全年的历史纪录。台湾对美国的出超（顺差）达1005.9亿美元，首次超越对中国大陆及香港的出超。 去年，美国就成为台湾最大的贸易出口国。今年美国更是台湾出口的第一大客户。 第六，美籍华裔女子张婉莹因涉监视台湾总统之子被FBI 抓捕。 10月4日，居住在美国加州尔湾的34岁房产经纪人张婉莹，准备搭乘前往上海的航班时，在洛杉矶机场被美国联邦调查局（FBI）探员逮捕。她被指控充当未注册的中共代理人，涉嫌监控在西雅图工作的台湾总统赖清德之子赖廷与。 FBI局长帕特尔（Kash Patel）在社交平台X上表示：“外国对手请注意，美国不再是你们可以安全从事间谍活动的地方。有人在美国领土上为中共监视外国领导人的家人，然后试图搭乘航班返回上海。调查局将追查任何威胁美国国家安全的目标，无论其藏身何处，都将绳之以法。” 二、为什么美台关系会有上述六大进展？ 主要原因可能有三： 第一，共享的价值观是连结台美最关键的基石。 10月7日晚，美国国务卿卢比奥在希腊雅典的帕特农神庙前发表了长达26分钟的演讲。这是一个对西方文明“寻根”的演讲，也是一篇在西方文明的源头试图复兴西方文明的檄文。 那么，西方文明的根本是什么呢？就是对上帝的信仰，以及在此基础上形成的自由、民主、法治、人权等价值观。 卢比奥演讲的核心是，呼吁美国及其盟友共同复兴这些在漫长岁月中被尘封、被遗忘、被扭曲、甚至被一些人抛弃了的核心价值观，回归常识、理性与传统。 10月10日，台湾总统赖清德在中华民国115周年国庆大典上，以“台湾山巅之城，地上的盐，世上的光”为题发表演讲。 “山巅之城，地上的盐，世上的光”，出自《圣经‧新约‧马太福音》，是耶稣对门徒的教导。其核心涵义是：人应以善行实践信仰，坚守良善，并以自身的言行为他人带来正面影响。 赖清德的演讲，与卢比奥的演讲相呼应，讲的都是回归对神的信仰，守护自由、民主、法治、人权的价值观。 美国是自由世界的领袖，台湾是以美国为首的自由世界的重要组成部分。共享的传统价值与普世价值，是把美台连结起来的最重要的基石。 第二，共同面临中共的挑战是美台携手合作的动力。 现在，美国面临的最大对手，就是中共；台湾面临的最大威胁，也是中共。 苏共解散、苏联解体后，中共成了全世界唯一的最大的共产主义政党、中共国成了全世界唯一的最大的共产主义国家。 上世纪90年代以来，中共利用以美国为首的西方国家对中共采取的绥靖政策，利用加入世界贸易组织的机会，利用西方的市场、资本、技术、金融、服务等，迅速成为世界第二大经济体。 美国是世界第一大经济体，中共是世界第二大经济体。习近平上台后，认为中共的“底气”足了，“东升西降”了，“时与势”在中共一边，“当今世界最大的乱源在美国”，“美国是我国发展和安全最大的威胁”，于是，开始在全球范围内跟美国争夺霸主地位。 2020年大瘟疫大爆发后，中共发起对美国的新冷战。标志性的事件有五：第一，1—2月，中共军舰挺进太平洋中部的中途岛军演。第二，3月，宣布南海战略核潜艇的“堡垒海区”建成。第三，6月，宣布对美国太空战部署完成。第四，7月开始，从渤海到黄海到东海到南海到内地，发起40多年来最密集的军演。第五，8月25日，《人民日报》发表批判美国的长文，中心思想是：美国最坏，“中共国”最好。 同一年，中共在暴力镇压香港反送中运动后，在香港强推“港版国安法”，提前27年终结了香港的“一国两制”，以中共“一党专政”取而代之。 同一年，中共在拿下资本主义的香港之后，立即将目标瞄准资本主义的台湾，在渤海、黄海、台海、南海发动了有史以来最密集的军演，开始对台湾极限施压，企图以中共的一党专政取代台湾的自由民主。 中共若拿下台湾，决不会止步。接下来，就是以台湾为据点，近处威胁日本、韩国、菲律宾等，更大范围将突破美国在二战后设立的防卫共产主义扩张的第一岛链，进而直接威胁资本主义的美国，建立一个以中共为主导的“人类命运共同体”。 中共所谓的“人类命运共同体”是什么？就是中共老祖宗马克思讲的“解放全人类”的另一种说法。 中共为什么在拿下资本主义的香港之后，要拿下资本主义的台湾，并与资本主义的美国争夺世界霸权呢？ 因为中共的老祖宗马克思仇恨资本主义、反对资本主义、必欲战胜资本主义，最后要取代资本主义，建立社会主义、共产主义的一统天下。 台湾处在西方的自由民主与中共的专制极权对峙的最前沿。美国则在全球范围内，从雅典，到罗马，到美洲大陆，面对着中共无孔不入的渗透与颠覆。 守护台湾，就是守护美国，守护自由民主。 如何守护？ 在投资、能源、无人机生产、科技、经贸、打击中共间谍上，全面合作，深度融合，你中有我，我中有你，共同筑起对抗共产主义的铜墙铁壁，乃必然之道。 第三，世界第一强国与世界最强劲经济增长体的强强联手。 美国是当今世界上的第一强国。美国强在哪里？首先，美国人民享有信仰自由、言论自由、免于恐惧的自由、免于匮乏的自由；其次，美国的国父们给美国留下了一个防止专制独裁极权的有效的分权与制衡的民主政治制度；再次，在自由民主的基础上，美国有世界上最发达的科技，最强大的军事实力，最具影响力的金融，最优秀的人才资源，最有消费能力的庞大的市场等。 台湾是当今世界上经济增长最强劲的地区之一。 据国际货币基金组织（IMF）2026年10月发布的《世界经济展望》报告，台湾2026年的实质GDP增长率预测被大幅上调至10.7%，这一增长率不仅在亚太地区高居榜首，也使台湾成为全球范围内极为罕见的实现双位数增长的经济体。 这一增长速度远超全球绝大多数主要经济体。美国预测增长为2.3%，中国预测增长为4.5%，欧元区预测增长为1.1%，印度预测增长为7.0%。 台湾作为全球经济增长最强劲的经济体，自然愿意与世界第一强国，实现强强联手了。 结语 现在总有人从川普与习近平关于台湾问题的谈话中揣摩美台关系的走向。其实，美台关系不在于川普怎么说，而在于美国政府与台湾政府实际怎么做。 现在有一个说法，台湾产业角色正从单纯的“Made in Taiwan”代工，转向以战略伙伴身份深度嵌入美方核心供应链，即“Made with Taiwan”。这个说法很有道理。 如今，美台正在投资、能源、贸易、科技、无人机、安全等各方面相互融合，形成一个共生共成、互利互惠、彼此守护的整体。 综上，尽管仍有各种挑战，美台合作的前景仍让外界看好。 大纪元首发

content: 2025年2月20日，诈骗园区的工作人员和来自中国的受害者抵达缅甸妙瓦底镇东部的缅泰边境检查站。（ STR/AFP via Getty Images） 【大纪元2026年10月14日讯】2026年的十一假期期间，中国大陆有人在赴泰国后接连离奇失踪。其中两起失踪案因为有比较具体的细节，在网络曝光后引发了广泛关注。 38岁的IT工程师胡星是九江人，他与35岁的宋华婷随亲属在十一期间一起赴泰旅游。10月6日，他们在泰国外出后失联，最后一次定位显示在泰缅边境的达府，照片里是一辆皮卡车和一片树林，此后他们便如人间蒸发，至今下落不明。泰国警方判断，两人可能已被转至缅甸。10月10日，心急如焚的家属联系中共驻缅甸大使馆求助，然而，得到的却是中共工作人员的推诿——“由家属联系核实”。 无独有偶，同一个假期，34岁的自由摄影师、山西人韩少杰，接到了一份“日薪四五千元、前往泰国拍摄”的工作邀约。对方打着“央视旅拍项目”的旗号，将他诱骗至曼谷。不料，他落地泰国仅一天，便直接失联。家属称，10月7日他发来一段语音，说自己上了黑车，醒来后被抢劫一空，已被人贩卖；次日又有一通疑似他本人的来电，要求家属支付15万元赎金，并警告家属不要报警立案，称“你们越闹我越遭罪”。韩的姐姐全网大声疾呼，恳求各界尽快营救。 值得注意的是，据韩少杰家属发布的寻人帖和他朋友的发帖，他曾参与央视纪录片拍摄，还曾在中共武警部队服役。10月11日，最新消息传来，韩少杰的姐姐宣布弟弟已安全回国。然而，与之前全网求助时所不同的是，韩女士在社媒上表示，“配合相关部门处理，不再过多公开细节。”那么，人究竟是怎么回来的？这背后，到底有着怎样的黑幕？ 一、“央视”成了诈骗招牌：中共的不作为与选择性失明 在韩少杰的遭遇中，最令人惊愕的地方，莫过于犯罪分子所使用的诱饵“央视旅拍项目”了。 据大陆“极目新闻”转述的家属说法，韩少杰是在拉萨期间，接到一个“朋友”的工作邀约，机票由家人代付，人是自己飞到曼谷的。也就是说，他在国内时就已经被盯上了。那么，发出邀约的人是谁？人现在哪里？此人是被利用的中间人，还是邪恶集团的同伙？至今中共没有给外界任何交代。 众所周知，中共的监控体系号称全球最严，“天眼”、大数据追踪、言论审查，几乎无处不在。在大陆，普通民众在网上说一句敏感的话，其账号可能很快被封禁，甚至会被警察找上门“喝茶”，更甚者直接被中共抓捕。 那么，针对犯罪分子公然打着“央视”的招牌，发布高薪招募诱骗受害人的犯罪事实，中共无孔不入的审查与追踪系统怎么就不能发挥作用、给公众一个及时的交代呢？ 中共对眼皮子底下行骗的黑色产业链视而不见、放任自流，无疑是对犯罪的纵容，是这类罪恶能够在大陆一路畅通的主要原因，必将导致更多大陆民众成为被绑架勒索的受害者。 二、韩少杰家人“不再公开细节”：谁害怕真相见光？ 2025年初，男演员王星被诱拐至缅甸妙瓦底事件曾引发舆论哗然。此后，中共高调联合东南亚国家展开打击，营造出电诈园区问题正被解决的假象。 然而，现实给了中共一记响亮的耳光。仅仅过了一年多，据缅甸媒体报导，妙瓦底一带被毁的部分园区又修复运作，附近的山区还冒出了新的据点。有反诈博主在交克村附近的草丛里，拍到成堆被丢弃的手机，疑似来自被骗去园区的年轻人的。如今，韩少杰、胡星、宋华婷等人的接连离奇失踪，更是直接打脸中共的高调作秀。 有网友表示，韩少杰的家属大概率是妥协并支付了15万元赎金，并且签了保密协议。不管真相如何，韩少杰被诱骗、囚禁、勒索，这是针对中国民众的恶性重大犯罪，绝不应该被当成一件个人“家事”悄悄私了。 究竟是谁冒用央视名义发出的邀约？韩少杰到底被转移到了哪里？有没有被劫持到哪座黑园区？他是怎么脱离险境的？15万元赎金到底给没给？这一连串的问题，公众绝对有权知道答案。到底，是谁在急着封口？又是谁害怕真相见光？ 其实，无论有没有交赎金，此事件都已经戳破中共所谓打击电诈的宣传谎言。中共必然希望降温处理，直接插手此事以压低事件的热度，这或许就是韩少杰家属所谓“配合相关部门处理”的背后原因吧。 三、中共大使馆让失踪者家属自己去“联系核实”的背后 在胡星与宋华婷失联后，家属在泰国报案之余，赶忙向中共驻缅甸大使馆求助。然而，据大陆“极目新闻”报导，中共使馆工作人员给出的回应竟是“需由家属联系核实”。 想想看，这难道不荒唐吗？亲属大概率已被拐过边境线，甚至被送进了缅甸的黑园区，对面就是手握枪械的血腥犯罪网络。一个普通老百姓拿什么去“核实”？向谁去“核实”？正常国家的领事保护，本应是海外公民遭遇危难时最后的安全屏障。而中共却直接把救人的责任甩给了受害者家属。人们不禁要问：洗脑电影《战狼2》里那句响当当的“在你身后，有一个强大的祖国！”不就是一张忽悠老百姓的空头支票嘛？ 更令人心寒的是，这场所谓的“救援”，比拼的似乎是舆论的热度。2025年初的男演员王星案，因其作为公众人物并有演艺圈背景，在全网掀起舆论海啸，中共迫于巨大的政治压力才不得不快速行动并收场；这次能够脱险的韩少杰，身上同样带着“央视纪录片”“退役武警”等极具话题热度的流量标签。那么，他的获救是否跟热度有直接关系呢？这不禁让平头百姓胡星和宋华婷的家人感到绝望，没有热度、没有名气，该怎么救他们？ 有分析认为，中共公安、领馆与电诈园区的大佬之间，似乎存在着某种默契。那些对舆论影响力大的，就私下处理、收钱放人，息事宁人；相比之下，那些声量微弱、关注度相对低的普通人，就任其在园区或黑窝中自生自灭。 如此看来，那就不只是“不作为”这么简单了，而是一场更可怕的官匪勾兑。美国司法部的一份起诉书，可以让我们从中窥见一斑。 四、美司法部起诉书显示：中共是电诈园黑链条的后盾 2025年10月，美国司法部公布了对太子集团董事长陈志的起诉书，并申请没收他名下约12.7万枚比特币，价值约150亿美元。司法部称，这个集团在柬埔寨经营着至少十个靠强迫劳动运转的诈骗园区，从全球受害者手里掠去了数十亿美元的巨额资金。 美司法部起诉书披露，陈志曾向他人吹嘘，自己与中共国安之间，有“付款换取预警通报”的安排。据起诉书所述，2023年5月，一名中共公安部官员表示，能让太子集团成员摆脱麻烦，而集团高层则是许诺关照该中共官员的儿子。这个集团高层还得意炫耀，每回诈骗园区遇上官方的打击，他们总是能提前收到通报，因此安然无恙。 更耐人寻味的是，2026年1月，陈志在柬埔寨被捕，但他并没有被送去美国的法庭，因为中共公安部先下手了，指控他涉嫌诈骗、开设赌场等罪名，并以此为借口将其带回大陆。要知道，陈志可是被美国司法部指控与中共国安部门有“付款换通报”安排的人，中共早不抓晚不抓，偏偏这个时候抓，很显然是为了避免这桩敏感的案子在国际法庭上被公开审理，以免中共的丑恶被曝光。 其实，那些官员收了黑钱，以中共政权的力量为罪恶黑产业链撑腰护航，电诈园区自然会更加肆无忌惮地行恶。不难想像，在那些没有任何约束的法外之地，更泯灭人性的罪恶也会随之发生。 五、黑产业链更大的罪恶——活摘器官 在东南亚电诈园区的重重黑幕背后，还隐藏着比诈骗和勒索更令人发指的罪恶，那就是活摘器官。 2026年10月，由中共公安部与央视联合摄制的纪录片《缅北电诈覆灭纪实》播出，片中幸存者唐某丰亲口讲述了自己在诈骗园区内被逼割肾抵债的噩梦经历。 无独有偶，2026年9月，泰国军方在清查靠近柬埔寨边境的黑产园区时，直接缴获了带有中文招牌的“中南医院”及神秘的专业手术台。泰军根据现场文件与设施推断，这些隐藏在园区深处的暗室，极有可能是被用于非法摘取器官的场所。 中国问题专家唐靖远表示，“这些电诈园区，本质上就是一个人矿处理中心，它是一个庞大的综合性的杀人工厂，里面包括黄、赌、毒、诈骗、绑架勒索、杀人、贩卖人体器官等等，每一个链条、每一个行业都是分工明确。”“电诈园区几乎全都是挂着那个‘一带一路’冠冕堂皇的招牌。” 将活人当器官供体，强摘器官牟取暴利，这样的罪恶并不是近年来才出现的。早在2006年，大纪元就首度曝光了中共大规模活摘法轮功学员器官的罪恶；此后的二十年时间里，大量证据表明，多年持续发生在中国大陆的活摘法轮功学员器官，是由中共主导，政府、司法、军警、医院等国家机器职能部门共同实施的反人类罪行。 2019年6月17日，由英国大律师杰弗里‧尼斯爵士主持的独立人民法庭，在伦敦宣布了终审判决：中共对以法轮功学员为主的良心犯进行大规模器官摘取，无可置疑地犯有危害人类罪以及酷刑罪。此判决将适用于世界各国、各地区政府、乃至国际法庭，在追究大陆参与强摘良心犯器官的组织或个人罪行的时候，都可直接采纳“独立人民法庭”的判决，无需再做调查取证。 2025年5月5日，美国国会众议院一致表决通过了《法轮功保护法案》（H.R. 1540）。这项法案由宾夕法尼亚州的共和党众议员斯科特‧佩里（Scott Perry）在国会众议院引入，旨在要求美国政府制止中共活摘法轮功学员器官的罪行，并要求美国对参与和协助活摘罪行的人员实施实质性的制裁。美国参议院则于2026年9月28日一致同意通过了《法轮功和活摘器官受害者保护法案》（S.4009）。 结语 韩少杰虽然侥幸虎口脱险，但胡星与宋华婷们至今依然下落不明，他们的家人仍在无声的绝望中煎熬着，还有更多被诱骗、绑架到东南亚的中国同胞依然生死未卜。 时至今日，依然有中国人接连赴泰后失踪。那些恶名昭彰的电诈园区，与大陆内部的黑恶势力里应外合。再结合美国司法部的起诉书，中共是电诈园区最大幕后保护伞的黑幕昭然若揭。这顶保护伞一天不拆除，电诈园区就一天不会真正消失；而作为活摘器官罪恶的始作俑者与最大推手，中共暴政一天不倒，这场针对广大民众的浩劫就不会停止。

title: 关键共和党众议员敦促国土安全部考虑废除中远海运进入美国港口的特权
summary: 美国众议院涉及美中关系、情报事务和交通运输的关键共和党议员致函美国国土安全部长，敦促审视中国远洋海运集团有限公司(COSCO)在美国港口所享有的特权。信中提到最近有媒体报道说，这家特大型中国央企在美国海岸线附近从事间谍活动。 众议院中国问题特设委员会主席约翰·穆勒纳尔(John Moolenaar)星期四(10月15日)宣布，他与众议院情报事务永久特设委员会主席里克·克劳福德(Rick Crawford)、众议院国土安全委员会运输与海事小组委员会主席卡洛斯·希梅内斯(Carl
content:
美国众议院涉及美中关系、情报事务和交通运输的关键共和党议员致函美国国土安全部长，敦促审视中国远洋海运集团有限公司(COSCO)在美国港口所享有的特权。信中提到最近有媒体报道说，这家特大型中国央企在美国海岸线附近从事间谍活动。

众议院中国问题特设委员会主席约翰·穆勒纳尔(John Moolenaar)星期四(10月15日)宣布，他与众议院情报事务永久特设委员会主席里克·克劳福德(Rick Crawford)、众议院国土安全委员会运输与海事小组委员会主席卡洛斯·希梅内斯(Carlos Gimenez)联名致函国土安全部长马克韦恩·马林(Markwayne Mullin)，要求该部审议中远海运加入美国海岸警卫队的“21世纪优质船舶计划”(Qualship 21)的资格。该项目允许在美国港口简化对合规外籍船只的检查。

这封在星期三发出的[信函](https://chinaselectcommittee.house.gov/sites/evo-subsites/selectcommitteeontheccp.house.gov/files/evo-media-document/finalized-scc-letter-to-dhs-re-cosco-shipping-qualship-21.pdf)提到了媒体最近有关中远海运的船只刺探情报的报道。

三位共和党众议员在信中说：“根据最近的公开报道，中远海运船只利用复杂和隐蔽的船上设备在我们的海岸附近拦截‘军事通信技术和加密研发”，构成严重的反情报威胁。报道进一步显示，这是中华人民共和国跨越几十年的长期谍报合作关系的一部分。”

这封信还说：“国有商船从事谍报活动，这是中国共产党常见的意料之中的背信行为。我们因此请求贵部迅速将中远海运船只从这份特权清单中除名，拒绝延长，并对代表人民解放军行事并作为中国工业基础一部分的类似公司实施额外的审查。”

三位共和党众议员在信中要求国土安全部提供一系列信息，包括：

1.   海岸警卫队是否从五角大楼、情报界或其他联邦机构收到有关中远海运及其船舶的情报数据或其他信息；
2.   海岸警卫队是否从情报界收到有关由中国或位于香港的公司拥有或运营、目前被列入或之前曾申请加入“21世纪优质船舶计划”的其他船只的类似情报；
3.   在五角大楼今年1月31日将中远海运认定为中国军事公司后，海岸警卫队是否因此对其船只持有的参加“21世纪优质船舶计划”的资格进行了审议；
4.   目前在决定给予或延长“21世纪优质船舶计划”资格时，是否会考虑某公司已被认定为中国军事公司或受到类似的国家安全认定的问题；
5.   对在美国辖区内的中远海运船只，海岸警卫队是否利用“港口国监督”(PSC)检查以外的权威，执行过或打算执行额外的登检，以应对据报道的间谍活动；
6.   鉴于香港缺乏有意义的自治，海岸警卫队是否考虑依据2019年生效的《香港人权与民主法》和其他相关法规，取消香港的“合格旗国主管机关”资格。

今年9月初，路透社援引匿名美国官员的话报道说，中国国有航运巨头中远海运的船只装有隐蔽装备，在北美、欧洲和亚洲海岸线附近为中国刺探包括美国在内的军事通信。报道说，美国官员提到中远海运和北京“几十年的情报收集合作”。

中远海运随后声称“上述言论没有任何事实依据”。该公司的声明还说：“中远海运集团始终在全球所有业务中坚持市场化运营和合规经营。”

中远海运在2025年1月被五角大楼列入中国军事公司名单。今年1月底，五角大楼对这份清单进行更新时，中远海运仍然榜上有名。

title: 端傳媒五項作品入圍第二十五屆卓越新聞獎
summary: 台灣卓越新聞獎基金會公布第二十五屆卓越新聞獎入選作品名單，端傳媒共有5項作品入選： 《香港宏福苑大火突發系列》入選平面及網路（文字）類特寫新聞獎 《馬太鞍堰塞湖洪災特寫系列》入選平面及網路（文字）類特寫新聞獎 《情色的未來系列》入選平面及網路（文字）類解釋報導獎 《淤泥下的光復鄉，塵土裡的人和地系列》入選新聞攝影類系列新聞攝影獎 《端聞》入選廣播及網路（音頻）類Podcast新聞節目獎 今年卓新獎參賽總件數為769件，經過評審團37位委員一個多月的審閱討論後，共選出94件入選
content: 台灣卓越新聞獎基金會公布第二十五屆卓越新聞獎入選作品名單，端傳媒共有5項作品入選： 《香港宏福苑大火突發系列》入選平面及網路（文字）類特寫新聞獎 《馬太鞍堰塞湖洪災特寫系列》入選平面及網路（文字）類特寫新聞獎 《情色的未來系列》入選平面及網路（文字）類解釋報導獎 《淤泥下的光復鄉，塵土裡的人和地系列》入選新聞攝影類系列新聞攝影獎 《端聞》入選廣播及網路（音頻）類Podcast新聞節目獎 今年卓新獎參賽總件數為769件，經過評審團37位委員一個多月的審閱討論後，共選出94件入選作品。除新聞志業特殊貢獻獎事先公布外，各獎項得獎名單將於11月17日頒獎典禮上揭曉。 卓越新聞獎基金會於2002年元月正式立案，成立宗旨在透過頒發年度新聞獎，為新聞倫理及新聞專業建立標竿。在此前，台灣新聞獎多由官方頒發，但許多新聞工作者都認為，媒體的重要工作之一，就是監督政府，因此由政府頒獎鼓勵新聞媒體，實非恰當。因此推動成立以「符合第四權邏輯」的民間新聞獎，取代過去難免威權政治殘餘的官方新聞獎舊格局。 端傳媒入選作品介紹 2025年11月26日，香港大埔宏福苑發生五級大火，消防處使用雲梯車撲救。攝：鄧家烜/端傳媒 《香港宏福苑大火突發系列》入選平面及網路（文字）類特寫新聞獎 ・《 解讀｜ 香港世紀大火：大埔宏福苑五級火至少44死，為何大火？如何救火？ 》 ・《 宏福苑世紀火災，香港人自發組織互助的三日三夜 》 ・《 解讀｜ 當高層建築發生火災：有何救援難點？災後如何調查和重建？ 》 香港大埔宏福苑大火是近年最嚴重的住宅火災，最終造成168人死亡。本系列三篇報導於災後72小時內刊發，為公眾提供及時資訊和解讀。 本系列在時間壓力下，深入及專業地報導了香港火災現場、制度問題，以及公民社會在打壓下的互助精神。報導在複雜多變的災難中兼顧了速度和深度，並將議題重新置於政治局勢的轉變中，帶出更真實的公共討論，為關注威權政府下人為災難如何被處理、能否問責的讀者提供第一手報導，以及整全的閱讀視角。 2025年9月26日，花蓮光復鄉大同村，阿美族婦女陳惠美回家，撫摸她留在家園的狗。攝：陳焯煇/端傳媒 《馬太鞍堰塞湖洪災特寫系列》入選平面及網路（文字）類特寫新聞獎 ・《 花蓮光復現場：馬太鞍溪堰塞湖溢流的那一日，他們為何沒走？ 》 ・《 堰塞湖洪災後的光復鄉：高齡化、外移與災難中的無人之地 》 ・《 「撒以責任」：洪災之後，阿美族百年制度讓Fata’an光復自己 》 2025年9月23日下午2時50分，花蓮馬太鞍溪堰塞湖壩頂溢流，洪水20分鐘內衝抵下游馬太鞍溪橋，半小時後沖毀該橋，泥流灌進光復市區，造成19人死亡、五人失聯、157人受傷，罹難者多為行動不便的長者，80歲以上至少八位。本系列三篇特寫從災難當下寫到災後兩個月，處理同一個問題：紅色警戒發出了，為什麼人還在屋裡。 報導沒有把責任推給「老人不聽勸」，而是逐層拆開：預警訊息如何在數位落差前失效、弱勢家庭為何連撤離都是奢侈、青壯年為何不在場，以及當所有官方系統同時失靈時，是誰把人一個一個找回來。 圖：Mantha Mok / 端傳媒 《情色的未來系列》入選平面及網路（文字）類解釋報導獎 ・《 AI是為了色情？從自用Deepfake到兒童性影像，四問科技與欲望的邊界 》 ・《 「有乳頭的車是性感的嗎？」當社群媒體成為色情守門人 》 端傳媒「情色的未來」系列報導，探當 AI 和演算法重塑情色內容的表達和流通，我們面對怎樣的法律和倫理難題，又如何在真實與幻象之間，重塑個體的慾望。 AI色情既是資本競逐的新前線，也是開源與黑客社群對平台審查的反抗實驗場，同時逼出深偽倫理、數據同意與未成年年齡辨識等法律難題。「情色的未來」系列不僅討論科技如何改變慾望，更從多元性別與性傾向出發，檢視演算法如何重塑可見與不可見的身體，並追問大型科技公司在內容審查與平台設計上的權力與責任。這是一組橫跨技術、法律與文化層面的完整系列報導，嘗試在 AI 時代為慾望與自由開拓更清晰的公共討論空間。 2025年9月29日，台灣花蓮光復鄉，災後街道仍堆滿淤泥，居民忙於清理，兩名居民於家門前觀望。攝：陳焯煇/端傳媒 《淤泥下的光復鄉，塵土裡的人和地系列》入選新聞攝影類系列新聞攝影獎 2026年1月5日，台灣新北市，人們在觀景台看風景。攝：陳焯煇/端傳媒 《端聞》入選廣播及網路（音頻）類Podcast新聞節目獎 「端聞」是一檔源自端傳媒編輯部的音頻新聞播客。每一期，我們選擇一則值得聽眾關心的新聞，邀請端傳媒的編輯、記者，特約記者或獨立撰稿人，透過緊密而有信息增量的新聞敘事，解釋新聞脈絡及其背後的議題，講述新聞之中的故事，聆聽人物與現場的聲音。 有些故事，不應被忽略 免費註冊端傳媒，與我們一起探索世界，理解時代。 立即註冊 # Meta推出强大开放AI模型 与中国企业展开竞争

脸书、照片墙和即时通信应用WhatsApp的母公司Meta周四（10月15日）发布人工智能开放模型Muse Spark Open，称其为美国迄今性能最强的同类模型。在这一由中国企业占据优势的领域，法国人工智能公司Mistral也正积极争夺市场。

发表时间： 15/10/2026 - 23:34

 6 分钟 浏览时间

 Illustration shows Meta Muse logo, keyboard and robotics hand REUTERS - Dado Ruvic

 作者： [安娜](https://rfi.fr/cn/%E4%BD%9C%E8%80%85/%E5%AE%89%E5%A8%9C/ "安娜")

广告

继续浏览后续

与ChatGPT、Claude等业内最先进的封闭模型不同，Muse Spark Open可供开发者下载、修改，并在自己的设备上运行。封闭模型则只能通过开发商提供的在线服务使用。

不过，这家社交媒体巨头仍未开放旗下最先进的模型Muse Wonder。该模型将于周一（10月19日）亮相。Meta首席执行官扎克伯格表示，Muse Wonder所属的模型系列，规模和先进程度均远超Muse Spark。此次发布的开放模型正是基于Muse Spark开发。

Meta人工智能业务负责人亚历山大·王周四在社交平台X上表示，Muse Spark Open是“迄今性能最强的美国开放模型”。不过，根据这家总部位于加利福尼亚州的公司自行开展的测试，其表现仍落后于中国最优秀的模型，包括月之暗面的Kimi K3和智谱的GLM 5.3。

今年春季发布的一份报告显示，过去一年，中国模型占专业平台“抱抱脸”模型下载总量的41%，超过美国模型。

这类开放模型成本较低，还允许企业根据自身需求进行调整，并将数据保存在自己的服务器上。

扎克伯格曾于8月承诺，将“很快”发布这一规模的开放模型。他坚信，让人工智能自由传播是防范其风险的最佳保障，这一立场与竞争对手Anthropic和OpenAI不同。

Muse Spark Open规模过大，普通电脑难以运行。Meta与苹果合作对其进行了优化，使其能够在两台高端Mac Studio电脑上运行。不过，其许可条款规定，营业额超过2000万美元的企业，如要向客户转售该模型的访问服务，必须与Meta签订协议。

今年，已有多家美国企业推出大型开放模型，争夺这一领域的市场，与中国企业展开竞争。除Meta外，这些企业还包括英伟达、OpenAI前首席技术官米拉·穆拉蒂创办的初创公司Thinking Machines，以及计划于本月发布Beam模型的Reflection AI。

法国Mistral则于10月初推出Mistral Large 4，并称其为美国和欧洲性能最强的开放模型。该模型的参数定于10月27日公开。

title: 菲律宾外交部驳斥中国驻菲大使井泉对马尼拉“动武”的威胁

content:
菲律宾外交部星期四(10月15日)发表声明，指责中国驻菲律宾大使井泉在向媒体发表谈话时用词不当，向马尼拉传递出一种“不加掩饰”的武力威胁。

“令人遗憾的是，中国大使井泉今天用词不当，似乎传达了一种不加掩饰的武力威胁；在菲中双边关系错综复杂的背景下，这种言论无助于事态发展。” 菲律宾外交部以负责海事事务的发言人罗赫利奥·维拉努埃瓦(Rogelio Villanueva Jr.)的名义发布的声明说。

井泉当天在菲律宾奎松市迪利曼学院(Diliman College)出席菲律宾-中国研究中心主办的第二届“迪利曼对话”期间接受记者采访时，发表了令菲律宾外交部不满的言论。

“如果我们想动用武力，可能很容易就能获胜。但我们不会这样做，我们不会动用武力。要知道，我们热爱和平。”井泉说。

菲律宾外交部在声明中指出，尽管各方立场存在分歧，但外交工作需要“讲究策略与克制”，以维护对话与接触的空间。

“希望所有派驻菲律宾的外交官在发表公开声明时更加审慎用词，以免进一步损害互信，或破坏对话与建设性接触的推进。”菲律宾外交部的声明说。

井泉发表争议性言论之时，中国和菲律宾在南中国海争议海域的摩擦与对峙仍然有增无减。

菲律宾军方10月8日试图从第二托马斯浅滩(Second Thomas Shoal，中国称仁爱礁，菲律宾称阿云津礁) 的“马德雷山”号(BRP Sierra Madre)军舰上撤离一名生病的菲律宾军人，但是此举遭到中方海警船的阻挠。

菲律宾海岸警卫队指责中国海警船阻挠紧急撤离行动，其中包括使用高压水炮，试图阻止菲律宾巡逻船抵达该浅滩，以接回生病的执勤人员。

菲律宾海岸警卫队发言人、海军少将杰伊·塔里埃拉(Jay Tarriela)当时表示，[这起事件](https://x.com/jaytaryela/status/2108154733773152314)导致任务延误了近10小时，并迫使菲律宾船只出于安全原因撤离，尽管高压水炮并未击中该船。

生病的执行人员最终在距离第二托马斯浅滩较远的一处汇合点被橡皮艇转移撤离，据报目前病情稳定。

南中国海是全球海上运输的一条关键水道，每年通过南中国海运输的国际贸易价值三万亿美元。中国政府声称根据其历史权利，拥有几乎整个南中国海的主权，尽管海牙国际仲裁法院在2016年的一项判决中已经否定了北京的主权主张。

主张拥有南中国海全部或部分主权的国家和地区除了中菲两国外，还包括越南、马来西亚、文莱和台湾。目前南中国海局势大体上平静，但是中国与菲律宾在南中国海争议海域的对峙和对抗却有愈演愈烈之势。

美国和菲律宾在1950年代签署了一项共同防御条约。美方官员一再表示，一旦菲律宾机舰和公务船在南中国海遭到袭击，美国便有协防菲律宾的义务。菲律宾除了加强与美国的军事安全关系外，还持续扩大其朋友圈，不断与日本、澳大利亚、法国、加拿大、欧盟及其他西方国家加强经贸和安全关系。

但是中国在南中国海争议海域的强势行径仍然没有任何收敛的迹象。

菲律宾国防部长吉尔伯托·特奥多罗(Gilberto Teodoro Jr.)星期三曾表示，出于安全考虑，菲律宾与中国军方的军事热线信已被暂停。他并指责北京滥用热线并扭曲通话内容。

井泉星期四发表谈话时也对此作出反应，声称如果菲律宾不恢复与中国的军事热线，将面临更大的对抗风险。

“并不是中国在请求菲律宾进行对话或开展两军沟通。如果你们不想跟我们谈，那也行，但吃亏的是你们自己，”井泉说，“你们将面临更高的对抗与冲突风险。”

菲律宾海岸警卫队发言人塔里埃拉星期四也指责井泉对菲律宾进行“直接威胁”，并驳斥了他关于中国热爱和平的说法。

“如果一位客人提醒主人说他其实可以轻易痛打对方一顿，却‘大发慈悲’决定不这么做，这绝非在描述友谊。他这是在威胁那个接待他的国家，甚至还要求我们对此心存感激，”塔里埃拉说。

Why Losing a Taiwan War Might Not Break China bbert@hudson.org Thu, 10/15/2026 - 14:43 SVG Commentary Oct 15, 2026 National Interest Why Losing a Taiwan War Might Not Break China The Yuan dynasty felt secure enough to invade Japan—and suffer catastrophic losses—because its position on the Eurasian landmass was secure. Is China’s today?   Ken Moriyasu Senior Fellow Ken Moriyasu Commentary Caption A truck drives through the Alataw Pass Comprehensive Bonded Zone in northwest China’s Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region. Located in the Mongolian Autonomous Prefecture of Bortala in Xinjiang, the Alataw Pass borders Kazakhstan. (Getty Images) Toggle Table of Contents Contents Contents Share to Twitter Twitter Share to Facebook Facebook Share to LinkedIn LinkedIn Share to E-mail E-mail Print Print Many Western analysts believe that a failed Taiwan operation could threaten Communist rule in China and that Chinese Communist Party General Secretary Xi Jinping therefore would not risk everything on such a high-stakes gamble. This hypothesis may or may not be true. But China’s own imperial history suggests another possibility. Over seven centuries ago, Kublai Khan, Great Khan of the Mongols and emperor of China’s Yuan Dynasty, launched two massive amphibious invasions of Japan. Both ended in failure. Yet Kublai remained on the throne, and the Yuan Dynasty survived for nearly another century. Why? Because the defeat at sea did not destroy the Yuan’s continental foundations of power. Today, the People’s Republic of China under Xi has approached its near-environs in Eurasia and the Pacific with a strikingly similar logic. That Xi hopes to bolster China’s power in the Pacific is hardly a secret. Yet under an increasingly continental conception of strategy, Beijing is also building sources of power that extend far into the Asian landmass. The United States and its allies need to grasp this continental dimension of Chinese power, so as not to overlook the larger strategic system that could allow Beijing to take risks at sea. The Mongol Empire was first forged on the high steppe under Genghis Khan, and consolidated in China under his grandson Kublai Khan. Kublai ruled China as emperor of the Yuan Dynasty (1271–1368), establishing his capital in present-day Beijing. It was under the Yuan that the far-flung regions of Tibet and Yunnan were brought under Chinese rule. At the same time, the Yuan Emperor, as Great Khan, claimed nominal supremacy over the other Mongol khanates ruled by members of his extended family: the Golden Horde in what is now southern Russia, the Chagatai Khanate in Central Asia, and the Ilkhanate centered on Iran. Together with tributary and vassal relationships extending into Korea and parts of Southeast Asia, this gave the Yuan court a political horizon that stretched far beyond China proper, deep into the Eurasian continent. The Han-led Ming Dynasty, which succeeded the Yuan in 1368, cast the Mongols as barbarians and rhetorically distanced itself from their rule. Yet in strategic practice, the continental focus the Yuan brought to Chinese foreign relations endured. Yongle, the Ming’s third emperor, repeatedly led armies deep into Mongolia , competing with the descendants of Genghis Khan to shape the balance of power across the Eurasian steppe.   Modern China’s behavior echoes this continental strategic logic. Like the Ming, the rhetoric of Xi’s China has hedged towards a promotion of Han nationalism . However, like the Yuan before it, the modern Chinese state has devoted enormous resources to securing its land frontiers, strengthening political and economic ties across Central Asia, and building infrastructure that binds China more closely to the Eurasian interior. In both the medieval and modern cases, security on the Asian continent provides the strategic depth that allows the Chinese state to devote greater attention and resources to its maritime periphery.  Divine Winds, Medieval and Modern  In War on the Rocks , we argued that Eurasia, not just the Indo-Pacific, will be crucial to the next phase of Taiwan deterrence. We focused on the trade and energy corridors that China is building across the Eurasian landmass, as well as Beijing’s engagement with crucial swing states along those routes. Pipelines and railways traversing the continent are less vulnerable to US maritime power than maritime routes, and could provide China with alternative economic and energy lifelines in a contingency such as a war over Taiwan.  The Belt and Road Initiative’s overland component is oriented toward Inner Asia and evokes the Silk Road caravans of the 13th-century Pax Mongolica , when Mongol rule facilitated the movement of merchants, goods, technologies, and ideas across much of Eurasia. Under Kublai, Beijing sat at the eastern end of a vast political and commercial network extending through Mongol-ruled territories far into the continental interior.  Why does this matter for Taiwan? Kublai offers a history lesson.  In the late 13th century, the Yuan launched naval expeditions as far afield as Japan and Java as Kublai sought to extend his authority beyond China’s shores. It was the failed invasions of Japan, during which storms devastated the Yuan-led fleets, that gave rise to the Japanese legend of the kamikaze , or “divine wind”—later lending its name to the notorious World War II suicide attacks, but predating them by centuries. To prepare for the invasions, Kublai mustered thousands of soldiers and sailors for both the 1274 campaign and the far larger second campaign in 1281. Korea supplied much of the fleet for the first invasion, while in 1281 Yuan forces launched a two-pronged assault on southern Japan involving Chinese and Korean ships and troops . Kublai’s secure position on the Asian mainland gave him the strategic depth to undertake these expeditions at enormous cost in personnel and materiel.  Logistical difficulties, Japanese resistance, storms, and the inherent limitations of premodern warfare ultimately thwarted Kublai’s ambitions against the shogunate. Yet the very fact that he could mount two such expeditions demonstrates both the resources at his command and the importance the Yuan attached to the effort. Despite these military failures, the dynasty survived for nearly another century. Its collapse in the late 14th century was not due to the sorts of major military invasions that had featured in its rise, but rather to popular rebellions that arose from domestic mismanagement.  Ultimately, the Yuan was able to sponsor significant overseas campaigns against Japan and survive their failure because it could absorb the losses without jeopardizing its position at home. It was the preeminent continental power in Eurasia , with no significant rivals capable of threatening its northern Chinese heartland.  Seven centuries later, the Communist Party today has staked much of its political capital on the promise of “reunifying” the Chinese nation, tying that goal to Xi’s broader project of national “ rejuvenation .” Taiwan occupies a far more central place in the Chinese Communist Party’s conception of sovereignty and national rejuvenation than Kublai’s Japan campaigns, which were about imperial expansion. A defeat over Taiwan would therefore carry political stakes far greater than those of Kublai’s failures. Yet extraordinary shocks do not necessarily produce regime change. The Chinese Communist Party has already survived civil war, world war, the Cultural Revolution, and the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests . It should not be assumed that a failed Taiwan operation would automatically trigger regime collapse in China. Disrupting the “Khanate” in Inner Asia  Modern China differs from Mongol China in another way. Unlike the Yuan Dynasty, which sat at the center of a broader political order across Eurasia, today’s China must actively compete with the United States and other powers for influence across the continent. While we offer a broader set of recommendations for strengthening that competition in our War on the Rocks piece, here we propose a narrower set of administrative changes within the US government. The objective is to place Central Asia at the heart of America’s China strategy.  Our first recommendation is to move military responsibility for the five Central Asian republics—Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, Turkmenistan, and Tajikistan—from the US Central Command (CENTCOM) to the newly renamed US Pacific Command (USPACOM). All five currently fall under CENTCOM , lumped in with the greater Middle East from Egypt to Pakistan. It is time to stop viewing Central Asia primarily through the legacy of US operations in Afghanistan and instead see the region through the prism of long-term strategic competition with China. Making the USPACOM commander responsible for Central Asia would integrate the region into planning for Pacific contingencies and encourage planners to consider how developments along China’s continental periphery could affect Beijing’s calculations over Taiwan.  Second, the undersecretary of defense for policy should shift responsibility for the five Central Asian republics to the assistant secretary for Indo-Pacific security affairs—and establish a dedicated office for Central Asia and Mongolia, headed by a deputy assistant secretary for Inner Asian affairs. A new Inner Asia office would consolidate expertise and give the region an institutional advocate able to assess Central Asia not simply as an adjunct to other theaters, but as a strategic arena in its own right.  Third, the same logic should extend to the State Department and Congress. At State, Central Asia should be severed from the Bureau of South and Central Asian Affairs and brought into the bureau responsible for East Asia and the Pacific, aligning the diplomatic and defense bureaucracies around the same strategic geography. Congress should similarly pair Central Asia with East Asia and the Pacific rather than South Asia. Washington needs to adapt to the geopolitical reality that Central Asia is no longer primarily an adjunct to stabilizing Afghanistan, and is strategically distinct from the maritime-oriented Indian subcontinent: it is increasingly part of the China challenge, and must be treated accordingly. If the United States wants to deter a modern Chinese maritime campaign against Taiwan, it should draw a lesson from medieval China’s maritime failures more than 700 years ago. A continental power’s willingness to accept risk at sea depends on the security and resilience it enjoys on land. If Beijing does not like what it sees in the west—courtesy of thoughtful and well-executed US policy planning—it may have second thoughts about moving east. Read in National Interest.
